title: TestForge: Benchmarking LLM-Based Test Case Generation
authors: Marco Vieira; Bhavain Shah; Priyam Ashish Shah
venue: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Analysis, Evolution and Reengineering (SANER)
abstract: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a well-established practice for building reliable software, yet its adoption is often limited by the effort required to write tests before implementing functionality. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate test generation directly from natural language specifications. However, systematic evaluation is still needed to assess their reliability. We present TestForge, a benchmarking framework for systematically evaluating LLM-based test case generation, which defines the core evaluation components in line with well-established benchmarking principles. As a first instantiation, we apply TestForge to JUnit 5 test generation for Java (version 11.0.6) programs, using a curated subset of the IBM CodeNet dataset that provides problem statements along with reference solutions. Our study encompasses problems ranging from basic algorithms to more complex scenarios, and it explores three prompting strategies: zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought. Results indicate that while LLMs can reliably produce functional tests for well-defined problems, they still struggle to generate tests that capture semantic depth and behavioral diversity.

abstract: We present an exploratory study investigating the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate Alloy formal specifications from both requirements documentation and production source code, and to derive executable test cases from those specifications. We evaluate on two real open-source Python libraries: Flipper, a feature flag management system, and Cerberus, a data validation library. title: Mutation Testing in Practice: Insights From Open-Source Software Developers

abstract: Mutation testing drives the creation and improvement of test cases by evaluating their ability to identify synthetic faults. Over the past decades, the technique has gained popularity in academic circles. In practice, however, little is known about its adoption and use. To fill this gap, this paper presents the results of a qualitative study among open-source developers on the use of mutation testing. Specifically, we report the results of a survey of 104 contributors to open-source projects using a variety of mutation testing tools. The findings provide insights into the main benefits and limitations of mutation testing. Overall, we observe a high degree of satisfaction with mutation testing across different programming languages and tools. Developers find the technique helpful for improving test-suite quality, detecting bugs, and improving code maintainability. Popularity, usability, and configurability emerge as key factors for adoption, whereas performance is the main limitation.

title: A Study of Flaky Failure De-Duplication to Identify Unreliably Killed Mutants
authors: Abdulrahman Alshammari; Paul Ammann; Michael Hilton; Jonathan Bell
venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation Workshops (ICSTW), Mutation 2024, 257–262
abstract: Mutation testing serves as a crucial technique for evaluating the efficacy of a test suite in identifying faults. However, non-deterministic behavior, particularly flaky tests, challenges confidence in mutation testing outcomes. Flaky tests introduce uncertainty when linking killed mutants to their causes, reducing trust in the assessment. This study examines the impact of flaky tests on mutant killing. Analysis of 22 Java projects previously examined for test flakiness reveals that 19% of mutants killed by these flaky tests result from flakiness introduced by at least one test. The study evaluates failure de-duplication approaches for distinguishing reliably killed mutants from unreliable kills and shows that this approach approximates the true number of reliably killed mutants at much lower computational cost than rerunning every test for every mutant.
v1_note: Nghiên cứu flaky tests và unreliable mutant kills; chưa đủ thông tin để xác nhận so sánh coverage và mục tiêu augmentation.
